title: AI Use in the Job Market Is Creating an Infinite Doom Loop
gist: A self-reinforcing 'AI doom loop' has formed in hiring: job seekers use AI to game suspected applicant-tracking-system (ATS) rankings while employers use AI to sort the resulting flood of near-identical applications, and evidence from a controlled Doist test suggests AI short-listing can systematically filter out the candidates who actually get hired and succeed.

insights.claim: A self-reinforcing dynamic has emerged in hiring where job seekers use AI to tailor résumés against suspected ATS screening, and employers deploy AI ranking tools to process the resulting flood of AI-optimized, near-identical applications, with each side's AI use making the underlying trust and matching problem worse rather than better.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Describes a structural, self-perpetuating dysfunction in the hiring market that undermines the value proposition of both job-seeker and employer-side AI tools, relevant to any thesis on HR-tech and recruiting-AI monetization.
insights.quote: We've got this tragic situation where each side has a problem. They're using AI to solve their own problem, but in ways that make the problem worse.
insights.locator: paragraph quoting Daniel Chait on the doom loop

insights.claim: ATS-optimization tools like Jobscan operate on the premise that hiring committees use AI to automatically rank and filter applicants, with only the top 10-20 percent ever considered, but this premise does not hold universally: some organizations still manage hiring entirely through human review regardless of company size or applicant volume.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Job seekers may be over-optimizing for an automated filter that doesn't exist at many specific employers, wasted effort that AI resume-tailoring vendors have limited incentive to correct.

insights.claim: Jobscan-style optimization services charge users roughly $30-50 per month, creating a potential conflict of interest since the company profits from continued subscriptions regardless of whether its scoring actually helps a candidate get hired and leave the job market.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Highlights a misaligned incentive structure worth flagging when evaluating consumer-facing job-search AI subscription products.

themes.theme: Evidence that automated screening misses good hires

insights.claim: Doist, a fully remote company with a large international applicant pool, tested AI short-listing on already-filled roles by feeding the original job descriptions and full applicant materials into an AI ranking tool; in the instances tested, the candidates who were actually hired and performing well roughly six months later did not appear on the AI's short list.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Concrete controlled evidence that automated ATS ranking can systematically filter out the actual best hires, a key due-diligence point for any company evaluating AI-driven ATS vendors and a caution against blind trust in AI hiring tools.
insights.quote: In two instances that we tested, the person we hired wasn't in the short list.
insights.locator: paragraph quoting Nadia Vatalidis of Doist

insights.claim: Toshiba's VP of HR reports that all applications are still reviewed by humans and that AI-polished materials don't materially help candidates pass its process, but she has noticed a rise in candidates using live AI assistance during interviews, detectable via pauses followed by unusually verbose answers.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Shows real-time AI use during interviews is now a widespread, employer-recognized phenomenon, likely to drive new detection tools and interview-format changes.
insights.locator: paragraph quoting Kim Jones of Toshiba

themes.theme: Job-seeker AI countermeasures and macro context

insights.claim: A design professional job seeker built his own AI-driven job-search system using Claude to comb, score, and log postings against his own criteria and salary requirements, effectively creating the inverse of an ATS aimed at the job seeker's own benefit, yet after months of intensive AI-augmented effort including a portfolio revamp, he still had no job offer.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Illustrates that sophisticated consumer-side AI augmentation of job search has not yet demonstrably improved outcomes, suggesting the addressable market for 'AI fixes my job search' tools may be overhyped relative to delivered results.
insights.locator: paragraphs on James Jacobsen's AI job-search system

insights.claim: Greenhouse CEO Daniel Chait frames the current dynamic as the first time in his experience that both job seekers and employers are simultaneously unhappy with the hiring process, a dysfunction amplified by a broader 'low-fire, low-hire' economy with scarce job postings and rising ghost-job/scam complaints.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Ties AI-driven hiring dysfunction to a broader soft labor market, a macro signal relevant to labor-market and HR-tech investment theses beyond the AI narrative alone.
insights.quote: This is the first time I can remember when both sides are unhappy. It's just not working.
insights.locator: paragraph quoting Daniel Chait near the end

insights.claim: Some US states are considering new laws to combat job-posting scams and 'ghost jobs' as trust in hiring processes erodes.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: A potential regulatory intervention point relevant to job boards and ATS platforms that could face new compliance requirements.
insights.locator: paragraph on ghost jobs and state laws
